title: Ambiguous fallback heuristic caused cross-region bounce and degraded capacity
creator: Nadia Kim
description:
Summary: On 2026-03-08 between 02:10 UTC and 03:30 UTC the routing plane entered a cross-region bounce pattern where a subset of requests were repeatedly rerouted between eu-west and us-central variants. Customer-facing symptom: elevated tail latency and increased token costs for affected tenants; a small percentage of requests (0.6% of global traffic) experienced multiple sequential reroutes and a several-second latency amplification. Impact: brief SLA misses for Dedicated customers in eu-west and intermittent spikes in host GPU utilization in us-central.

What happened (short timeline):
- 02:07 UTC: rolling rollout of routing policy change (policy-service v2.14.0) introduced a new "fallbackScore" heuristic that combines variant compatibility score and region distance penalty.
- 02:10 UTC: first reroute spike observed; policy-service returned a new fallback path for ~0.6% of requests.
- 02:12 UTC: KV cache eviction coincided with policy refresh; some routers had stale variant compatibility state while policy recommended a variant swap.
- 02:18-02:42 UTC: oscillation amplified due to short TTLs on per-request sticky metadata and lack of hysteresis in circuit-breaker evaluation.
- 02:45 UTC: mitigation applied (emergency toggle to disable fallbackScore mixing and force local-region preference).
- 03:00 UTC: traffic stabilized; follow-up analysis initiated.

Root causes (multi-factor):
1) Ambiguous fallback heuristic: the new fallbackScore blended variant-compatibility and region-penalty weights using a single comparator. In edge cases where compatibility scores were near-equal, small timing differences caused routers to prefer different variants, producing flip-flops across requests.
2) TTL mismatch and policy refresh race: policy-service publishes updates with a TTL shorter than some routers' sticky decision windows; combined with KV cache eviction this allowed different routers to operate on mismatched state for the same request path.
3) Missing hysteresis in circuit-breakers: breaker logic evaluated raw load metrics without a damping window, so transient spikes caused decisions to flip rapidly.
4) Incomplete telemetry for decision lineage: there was no per-request trace that captured both the policy input and the final variant selection in a single correlated span; this made it slow to reconstruct the flip sequence during the incident.

Immediate mitigations taken during incident:
- Emergency config: disabled fallbackScore mixing and reverted to explicit local-region preference for canary windows (applied at 02:45 UTC).
- Increased router sticky TTL to 60s from 10s to reduce rapid re-selection during policy churn.
- Throttled policy-service rollout and paused further policy pushes until validation checks added.

Longer-term corrective actions (action items):
- Implement deterministic fallback comparator with explicit precedence rules so equal-scoring variants cannot flip-flop (owner: Aaron Patel, estimate: 3, due: 2026-03-21).
- Align policy TTL semantics across publisher and router (add contract tests that assert TTL invariants) (owner: Mei Alvarez, estimate: 2, due: 2026-03-18).
- Add hysteresis / smoothing window to routing circuit-breakers (owner: Jonah Reed, estimate: 5, due: 2026-04-04).
- Create per-request decision lineage trace: attach policy-version, input-compatibility vector, and final variant id to request traces for 14 days (owner: Priya Desai, estimate: 8, due: 2026-04-11).
- Add gating tests to rollout pipeline: simulate policy churn vs. sticky TTLs and verify no oscillation (owner: QA Team, estimate: 5, due: 2026-03-28).
- Post-incident runbook: emergency toggle, recommended TTL ranges, and rollback flow; add to on-call runbook and schedule tabletop (owner: SRE Docs, estimate: 2, due: 2026-03-17).

Acceptance criteria:
- No flip-flop oscillation observed in the controlled canary replay for 72 hours with high synthetic churn.
- Traces for 100% of routed requests include decision lineage fields.
- Policy rollout pipeline rejects changes that would reduce effective TTL below router sticky window.

Notes and trade-offs considered:
- We rejected making region-penalty dominant by default because it would harm latency/cost trade-offs for workloads intentionally using cross-region variants for capacity reasons. Instead we will make comparator deterministic and surface explainability to the Console.
- Increasing TTLs reduces flexibility for fast rollouts; we will compensate by improving rollout gating and targeted rollouts per customer tier.
